newsitem.title: ITALY: Fiat set to reap benefits from industry incentives.
newsitem.headline: Fiat set to reap benefits from industry incentives.

text.p: Italian car giant Fiat, which holds the lion's share of a flagging domestic car market, will receive a welcome boost from a government plan to encourage motorists to trade in ageing cars for new ones, analysts said.
But while sales of Fiat's compact models are likely to jump, margins could come under pressure if the measures trigger a fresh round of discounting among top car manufacturers.

The government said on Monday that motorists who hand in cars on the road for more 10 years will be paid a bonus of 1.5 million lire ($1000) for cars with engines of less than 1,300 cc and up to two million lire for cars with larger engines.
"The experience with a similar incentive scheme in France is that you get intense price competition," said Gianluca Pediconi, an equities analyst with Milan brokerage Milla Sim.
Car manufacturers will have to match each bonus on offer with a discount for the same amount.

The decision to go ahead with a programme of incentives signalled an about-turn for Prime Minister Romano Prodi who had earlier said he was opposed to the idea on the grounds that it would not bring a lasting revival to the car market.
Pietro Marzotto, an influential industrialist who is chairman of his family's textiles group of the same name, criticised the government for adopting the measures.
"It leaves me very perplexed. Where stimuli of this nature have been introduced they have been of no use. You only have to look at France," Marzotto told Milan daily Corriere della Sera.

The car sales package came at the end of a year in which Italians have been faced with a rising tide of taxes and belt-tightening measures which have steadily eroded the purchasing power of salary earners.

All the leading volume car manufacturers -- among them Fiat, Renault, Peugeot, Volkswagen -- have been trying to woo Italian customers in recent months with generous discounts and zero-interest hire purchase schemes.

"In France we saw an orderly market become extremely disorderly as a result of incentive schemes," said Nicholas Potter, an auto industry analyst at Credito Italiano's London office. "But if car makers (in Italy) are imaginative one would hope there is some profit in the scheme for all participants," Potter added.

Italian car industry think tank Promotor estimates that the nine-month incentive plan, which comes into effect next week, will generate 200,000 extra sales. Total 1996 car sales are expected to number around 1.7 million.
Some analysts believe car sales could rise by even more, with Fiat expected to pick up around half the additional sales.
No other major European manufacturer enjoys such a dominant position in its home market as Fiat, which currently acounts for 44 percent share of Italian car sales.

"We think that in view of the French experience car sales could go up by as much as 300,000," said Pediconi, who believes turnover at Fiat's car making division, Fiat Auto, could rise by 2.5 to three trillion lire as a result.
Credito Italiano's Potter said Fiat's net group profit in 1997 could rise to more than two trillion lire from an estimated 1.18 trillion in 1996 on the back of the incentive scheme.
